subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the derivative dy/dx of the function y = [(1 − 2x)^(2/3)(1 + 3x)^(−3/4)]/[(1 − 6x)^(5/6)(1 + 7x)^(−6/7)].

mark_split.label: Say why logarithms are used here
Take logarithms and expand into four terms
Differentiate both sides term by term

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say why logarithms help when the function is a product and quotient of powers.

steps.label: Say why logarithms are used here
steps.margin_note: First mark. Here the powers are constants, so the product rule and quotient rule would work — but on four factors they take many lines. The logarithm changes multiplication into addition, and a sum of four terms is differentiated one term at a time.
steps.memory_tip: A logarithm turns multiply into add and divide into subtract. Four factors become four separate terms, and each one is easy.
lines: The function is a product and a quotient of four powers. Applying the product rule and the quotient rule directly takes many lines, and a term is easily lost part way through.
A logarithm turns a product into a sum and a quotient into a difference, and brings every power down in front. So take logarithms of both sides.
All four brackets must be positive for the logarithms to exist, which holds for −1/7 < x < 1/6.

recall.must_convey: That logarithms are used because they turn the product and quotient of four powers into a sum of four simple terms.
accept: take log on both sides because it turns multiplication into addition
log makes the quotient a subtraction
the powers come down in front of the logarithms
four factors become four separate terms
log teesukunte multiplication addition ga maruthundi
logarithmic differentiation is quicker than the product and quotient rules here

steps.why: This is logarithmic differentiation used for a different reason from the variable-power questions in this chapter. Nothing here forces the method, but it replaces one very long quotient-rule calculation with four one-line derivatives.
common_mistakes: Starting the quotient rule on the whole expression and running out of room part way through.
Saying the method is needed because the power rule fails, which is not true here — the powers are constants.

steps.label: Take logarithms and expand into four terms
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Watch the two negative powers. (1 + 3x)^(−3/4) is in the numerator, so its term is −(3/4)log(1 + 3x); (1 + 7x)^(−6/7) is in the denominator, so subtracting a negative gives +(6/7)log(1 + 7x).
steps.memory_tip: Numerator terms get a plus, denominator terms get a minus, and a negative power flips that sign once more.
lines: Bringing each power down in front,

recall.must_convey: That log y expands into the four terms with signs +2/3, −3/4, −5/6 and +6/7.
accept: log y is two thirds log one minus two x minus three fourths log one plus three x and so on
numerator terms are added and denominator terms are subtracted
the minus three by four power gives a minus sign in front
the denominator term with a negative power becomes positive
negative power vunte sign marchuthundi
four log terms with the fractions in front

steps.why: The negative exponents are what make this step worth two marks. A factor with a negative power really belongs on the other side of the fraction bar, and that shows up in the logarithm form as a change of sign.
common_mistakes: Giving all four terms a plus sign by forgetting that the denominator is subtracted.
Reading (1 + 7x)^(−6/7) in the denominator as a minus term, when the two minus signs make it plus.

steps.label: Differentiate both sides term by term
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The left side gives (1/y)(dy/dx). On the right each term needs the chain rule, so each one brings out the derivative of its own bracket: −2, 3, −6 and 7.
steps.memory_tip: Every log(bracket) differentiates to (derivative of the bracket) over (the bracket). The number in front of x is what comes out on top.
lines: Differentiating (1) with respect to x, using the chain rule on each term,

recall.must_convey: That each log term differentiates by the chain rule, giving the bracket derivative over the bracket, and the left side gives (1/y)(dy/dx).
accept: the left side is one by y into dy by dx
each log term gives the derivative of the bracket over the bracket
minus two comes out of one minus two x, three out of one plus three x
chain rule on every term
prathi log term ki chain rule vaadali
the inner derivatives are minus two, three, minus six and seven

steps.why: Each term is a constant times log of a linear bracket, so its derivative is that constant times the bracket's own derivative divided by the bracket. Writing the raw form first keeps the two minus signs visible before they are simplified away.
common_mistakes: Differentiating log(1 − 2x) as 1/(1 − 2x) and losing the −2 from the chain rule.
Writing the left side as dy/dx instead of (1/y)(dy/dx).

steps.label: Simplify the four coefficients
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Two of the four terms change sign here: (2/3)(−2) is negative, and −(5/6)(−6) is positive. The third and fourth coefficients cancel to whole numbers, 5 and 6.
steps.memory_tip: In the last two terms the fraction and the bracket derivative cancel exactly: 5/6 with 6, and 6/7 with 7. Only the first two stay as fractions.

recall.must_convey: That the four coefficients simplify to −4/3, −9/4, +5 and +6, so two of the terms are negative and two are positive.
accept: two thirds into minus two is minus four by three
five sixths into minus six is minus five, and the minus in front makes it plus five
six sevenths into seven is just six
the first two terms are negative and the last two are positive
five by six and six cancel ipothayi, five vasthundi
minus four by three minus nine by four plus five plus six

steps.why: This is where the answer's signs are settled. The third term has a minus in front and a minus inside, and two minus signs give a plus — the single most common place to lose a mark in this question.
common_mistakes: Keeping the third term negative by using only one of its two minus signs.
Writing −4/(3(1 − 2x)) as −4/3 − 2x, splitting a denominator that cannot be split.

steps.label: Multiply back by y
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Multiply both sides of (3) by y and write y back out in full, since the question gave y as an expression and not as a name.
steps.memory_tip: Logarithmic differentiation always ends the same way: multiply by y, then replace y with the original expression.

recall.must_convey: That both sides are multiplied by y and y is written back as the original expression.
accept: multiply both sides by y to get dy by dx
write y back as the original function
the answer is the original expression times the bracket
y ni malli original expression ga rasi multiply cheyyali
dy by dx equals y into the four term bracket
put the given function back in place of y

steps.why: The working found (1/y)(dy/dx), not dy/dx, so the answer is not complete until it is multiplied by y. Writing y out in full is what makes the answer a function of x alone.
common_mistakes: Stopping at (1/y)(dy/dx) and calling it the derivative.
Leaving the letter y in the final answer when the question defined y by an expression.

insider_note: Four fractional powers multiplied and divided, so take logarithms first — the product and quotient rules directly would run for pages. Each power becomes a coefficient times a simple log.
